caseno: Civil Appeal No. 11 of 1976 from the judgment of the High Court in Second Appeal No. 996 of 1964.
lawyer:
Khandker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, Advocate instructed by Abu Backkar, Advocate-on-Record -------  For the Appellant. 
Abdul Aziz, Advocate-on-Record ------- For the Respondent No. 1.
Ex-parte ------- Respondents 2 to 6.
parties:
Md. Altafur Rahman  ------- Appellant.
Vs.
Tamijur Rahman  ------- Respondent.
full_judgment:
5. The learned Single Judge of the High Court reversed the finding of the first appellate Court, and restored that of the trial Court in decreeing the suit. The learned Single Judge found that Tamijur Rahman, the son of plaintiff Pearjan has given a genealogy, which was not challenged in cross-examination, and that fact found corroboration from the recording of the khatian Ext.3. The first appellate Court, did not take note of the fact, that he was not cross examined on the authenticity of the genealogy. The learned Judge next, held that, the-impugned kabala in favour of appellant Altafur Rahman was under challenge, and it was a document executed by a purdahnasheen lady, and so the onus that the lady got independent advice as to the nature and effect of the transaction into which she was entering, and that she executed the document understanding its contents and the significance of the transaction, was upon the recipient of the document, the appellant. The learned Munsif was right in discarding the evidence of D.W.7 Akmal Ahmed, whose demeanour was recorded by him, as suspicious, as he evaded the question, and would not answer directly. He was the lone witness, who is supposed to be the person who gave independent advice. Therefore, there was no evidence of independent advice to the lady. As to the voluntary execution of the document by Ashrafjan, the learned Single Judge pointed out that D.W.2, appellant Altafur Rahman, D.W.4 Matiur Rahman an attesting witness, and D.W.7 Akmal Ahmed were relied upon by the Court of appeal below. He then discussed the evidence of D.W.2, D.W.3, the scribe, D.W.4, and attesting witness along with other evidence namely, that of D.Ws. 5, 6 and 7, and found serious discrepancies in their evidence. He noted the low valuation of the land, a fact admitted by the defence, and considered the reasons for selling the land by the lady. On a full discussion of all evidence, he held that the conclusion arrived at by the Munsif that the document was fraudulent and without consideration was to be preferred to that of the first Court of appeal. It was also held with reference to the evidence of D.W.2 that the suit was barred by limitation. 

 10. Mr. Khandker mainly concentrated his argument on other two issues. As to the question of the plaintiff's being heirs of Ashrafjan, he has very little to say, because the first Court of appeal, was patently wrong in assuming that the plaintiffs relied on khatian Ext.3, in proof of their genealogy. The High Court has rightly pointed out, the genealogy given by the first witness of the plaintiff Tamijur Rahman, was not challenged in cross-examination, and there is some support of his statement in the khatian. The errors committed by the lower appellate Court, are firstly, in assuming corroborative evidence as substantive one, and secondly, in ignoring the non-challenge in cross-examination of the essential evidence of genealogy given by the first witness of the plaintiffs. These are errors of procedure, committed by the first appellate Court, which have affected the merits of his finding on the issue of heirship of the plaintiffs with Ashrafjan. This error of law committed, by the lower appellate Court has given ample jurisdiction to the High Court to interfere.
